Title: SkillSafetyBench: Evaluating Agent Safety under Skill-Facing Attack Surfaces
Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a common interface for extending large language model agents, packaging procedural guidance with access to files, tools, memory, and execution environments.However, this modularity introduces attack surfaces that are largely missed by existing safety evaluations: even when the user request is benign, unsafe influence may reside in skill guidance, local artifacts, or executionenvironment files that steer the agent toward unsafe actions.We present SkillSafetyBench, a runnable benchmark for evaluating such skillfacing safety failures.SkillSafetyBench includes 155 adversarial cases across 47 tasks, 6 risk domains, and 30 safety categories, each evaluated with a case-specific rule-based verifier.Experiments with multiple CLI agents and model backends show that non-user attacks can consistently induce unsafe behavior, with distinct failure patterns across domains, attack methods, and scaffold-model pairings.Our findings suggest that agent safety depends not only on model-level alignment, but also on how agents interpret skills, trust workflow context, and act through executable environments.The complete benchmark is available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/ skill-safety-bench.
Major_Contribution_Result: SkillSafetyBench is a runnable benchmark of 155 adversarial cases across 47 tasks, 6 risk domains, and 30 safety categories, each with a case-specific rule-based verifier for skill-facing non-user attacks under benign user requests. Across CLI agents and model backends, non-trivial ASRs appear; overall ASR reaches 50.3% for Codex+GLM-5.1 and 49.7% for Kimi Code CLI+Kimi-K2.5, while Claude Code+Opus-4.6 has the lowest overall ASR at 15.5%. Average ASR is highest in RD1 (58.7%), then RD2 (49.3%), RD5 (46.6%), and RD4 (41.6%).
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Scope is intentionally limited to skill-facing local non-user attacks expressible via skill materials/local artifacts and verifiable from execution evidence; it does not cover the full agent-safety space. Authors note needs for more interactive multi-turn settings, longer-lived evolving skill ecosystems, and that rule-based verifiers are less suited to diffuse failures needing broader semantic or human assessment. Dual-use risk of adversarial cases is acknowledged.
Critics: The benchmark is strong for artifact-grounded skill/local-context attacks on coding CLI agents, with rule-based verifiers reducing judge ambiguity. Coverage is specific to the authors' 155 cases and scaffolds, so ASR rankings are not transferable to unrelated tool-agent suites. It advances evaluation of non-user attack surfaces that many endpoint-text benchmarks miss.
